caption:
Russian prank duo Vovan and Lexus posed as Ukrainian security official Rustem Umerov on a 17-minute video call with three OpenAI national security officials.
They talked about OpenAI's possible help for Ukraine's military. Then the pranksters posted the recording online.
OpenAI says it investigated weeks ago, concluded it was a prank and took steps so it cannot happen again.

Should AI companies discuss military work on a video call at all?

Follow @neurafeed.ai for daily AI news.

Source: The Intercept · Photo: Roy Rochlin/Getty Images for Semafor
threads_text: Russian pranksters posed as a top Ukrainian security official and got three senior OpenAI national security staff on a 17-minute video call about military AI. paragraphs.text: Three senior OpenAI national security officials spent 17 minutes on a video call with a man they believed was Rustem Umerov, a senior Ukrainian security official, according to a report The Intercept published on November 11, 2026. The caller was in fact part of Vovan and Lexus, a Russian comedy duo known for prank calls, and the pair later posted a recording of the conversation online.

OpenAI spokesperson Nate Evans told The Intercept that the company had opened an investigation into the call's authenticity weeks earlier, worked internally and with the relevant authorities, and concluded that it was a prank. He said OpenAI had taken action to prevent similar situations in the future. The company did not say when the call took place or which measures it adopted, according to Digit.

The OpenAI participants were Sasha Baker, who leads national security policy at the company and previously held a senior Defense Department post; Caroline Zier, OpenAI's lead for strategic initiatives, who also worked at the Defense Department; and Ben Crampton, who leads the company's European national security work and previously worked for the European Union and the United Nations, The Intercept reported.

Baker and Zier said during the call that they had met Umerov before. The impersonator appears to have kept his camera off. Vladimir Kuznetsov, one of the two pranksters, told The Intercept that the duo first reached a senior Ukrainian official in San Francisco while posing as Umerov, and that this official believed he was setting up a meeting with OpenAI.

The fake official asked about OpenAI's possible military support for Ukraine, including offensive capabilities. Crampton said the company wanted as deep a relationship with Ukraine as possible but might not reach that goal right away. He also described a general reluctance among many senior people at OpenAI about offensive military uses, and said offense and defense cannot always be told apart, according to accounts of the recording.

The officials mentioned Daybreak Blue, an OpenAI model that finds and fixes computer vulnerabilities, and a developing partnership with Ukraine's Ministry of Defense. Baker said OpenAI had been in contact with the Pentagon about helping Ukraine. When the caller asked whether OpenAI could help counter Elon Musk's influence, Baker said the company probably could not help with Musk.
Business Today, citing The Intercept, noted that OpenAI has an ongoing $200 million contract with the U.S. Department of War to supply AI applications for military users.

Vovan and Lexus are the pseudonyms of Vladimir Kuznetsov and Alexei Stolyarov, according to Digit. They have made prank calls to public figures since 2011, including Elton John and the late Senator John McCain. Their pranks often line up with Russian foreign policy, and they have been accused of working with the Russian government, which they deny. The Ukrainian Embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to The Intercept's request for comment.

The episode shows how much weight a familiar name and title can carry in a remote meeting. The call reached OpenAI through a real Ukrainian official, and two of the three participants believed they already knew the person on the other end. For an AI company that now works with defense customers, conversations about military uses carry far higher stakes than an ordinary sales call, and a caller with the camera off is a gap that formal identity checks can close without relying on recognition.

The next signal to watch is whether OpenAI or other AI labs describe the identity checks they now require before national security conversations, and whether Ukrainian officials explain how the introduction to OpenAI was arranged.
